reception.text: The General Land Office's annual report called the cavern "a cave whose beauty is probably second to no other in the United States."
reception.source: GLO Annual Report, fiscal year 1908, p. 19

reception.text: The River Press of Fort Benton ran a front-page Helena dispatch, "Montana's Mammoth Cavern," describing the cave chamber by chamber and reporting the new supervisor's appointment.
The Whitefish Pilot noted that Montana had a cave comparing favorably with Kentucky's Mammoth Cave, newly set aside by Roosevelt.

political_impact.text: Louis L. Sharp, chief of the General Land Office's field division, was named supervisor of the monument seven weeks after the signing.
A General Land Office survey found the 160 acres lay wholly within the Northern Pacific Railway's unpatented land grant, so the government had reserved ground it did not own.
Dan Morrison's attempt to secure title to the cave under the mining laws revealed the railway's ownership; there was no lawsuit.
political_impact.source: Sen. Thomas J. Walsh, Congressional Record, January 26, 1929

political_impact.text: The Northern Pacific quitclaimed the tract to the United States for the monument, on condition that it revert to the railway if the monument was no longer maintained.

legacy.text: By 1930 the cave was closed to visitors because of vandalism and the lack of funds for lighting and ranger protection.
legacy.source: NPS, Glimpses of Our National Monuments (1930)

legacy.text: Civilian Conservation Corps Company 574 developed the cave between 1935 and 1941, putting in the first electric lighting, a 538-foot exit tunnel, and a 3.2-mile road up Greer Gulch.
legacy.source: Lewis and Clark Caverns National Register nomination

legacy.text: Montana dedicated the state park on May 4, 1941; rain canceled the ceremony, but some three thousand people drove up anyway.
It is the only one of Roosevelt's eighteen national monuments that left federal ownership.

today.name: Lewis and Clark Caverns State Park
today.note: 3,015 acres; counted as Montana's first state park.

today.name: Lewis and Clark Cavern National Monument
today.note: Ended as a consequence of the 1937 conveyance to Montana, not by a formal abolition.

related.note: Jewel Cave, three months earlier, also used the Antiquities Act's scientific-interest reach to protect a cave.

later_actions.text: President Taft's Proclamation 1123 confirmed the same 160 acres on the new survey, subject to the railway deed's conditions.
A private act paid Dan A. Morrison $5,000 for the discovery, exploration and development of the cavern.
Congress authorized and directed the Secretary of the Interior to convey the monument and surrounding land, about 1,500 acres, to Montana for a public park, reserving minerals to the United States.

uncertain: Who chose the name "Lewis and Clark Cavern" is not known.
No individual sponsor of the monument has been identified.
What became of the railway's 1911 right of reverter when the land went to Montana in 1937 is not known.
The date the conveyance to Montana was completed is not known.
Whether Montana's 1908 dailies took any position on the monument has not been tested.
